They test the map by changing the room in the simulation and finding the row that stops matching. The break column records where the simulation gives exact numbers and the room does not.
stations.example: A thermostat simulation beside the heating system of their classroom.
stations.representation: A two-column table with parts as rows, plus a break column.
stations.challenge: Tests the map by changing the model and finds the row that fails. A model is a built description of the room, and students list where it differs from the room.

stations.move: Students build a three-way map of a spam filter (machine learning), a route finder (search) and a file-sharing network (distributed system). Rows: input, what changes, what it guarantees, who set the objective. For each pair of columns they write where the comparison breaks and what the system can be said to do without intention.
stations.example: A spam filter, a route finder and a file-sharing network.
stations.representation: A three-column table with four rows and a break cell for each pair.
stations.challenge: Maps three cases at once and states what each guarantees. Each break cell is written without intention words.

stations.move: Students map linear search and binary search for a name in a sorted list. Rows: input needed, steps for 10, 1,000 and 1,000,000 names, and what each guarantees. In the break column they state the input condition under which binary search gives a wrong answer, and justify a choice for a stated need.
stations.example: Linear search and binary search for a name in a sorted list.
stations.representation: A two-column table with step counts in the rows and a break column.
stations.challenge: Compares by how steps grow with input size, and names the input condition that breaks one method.

analogy.teachingPrompt: Which row matches in both cases, and what is the first thing that stops matching when you test the comparison?
gaps: Naming where an analogy breaks is untested with school students at K-2 and 3-5.
Look-alike features pull attention away from matching roles at every age studied, so the row cards at K-2 and 3-5 need to be tested for this.
Seventh and eleventh graders mostly treat a model as a copy, so the 6-8 and 9-12 break columns carry the weight and need classroom testing.

coverage.Data: Carried by Analogy, Causal and Tinbergen. Payoff Matrices scores pairs of rules and holds no recorded values to compare.
coverage.Information: Carried by Analogy Mapping at 6-8, counted in storage bits. A station at C1:9-12 that maps lossless against lossy compression of one message would add a second tool.
coverage.Representation: Carried by Analogy, Causal and Tinbergen. A payoff table has no stored form to compare.
coverage.Abstraction: Carried by Analogy (what a model leaves out), Causal (function boxes) and Tinbergen (what a chart leaves out). Payoff Matrices cannot carry it.
coverage.Decomposition: Carried by Causal (functions as boxes) and Tinbergen (a remix history). Analogy and Payoff have no natural place for splitting a problem.
coverage.State: Carried by Causal and Tinbergen. A map of stored values and a trace are the natural tools. Analogy and Payoff would only repeat them.
coverage.Search: Carried by Analogy, Tinbergen and Payoff. Causal Mapping has no stage where search is the main idea.
coverage.Machine Learning: Carried by all four tools, but only at 9-12 because the space introduces it there.
coverage.Feedback: Carried by all four tools from 6-8 on.
coverage.Distributed System: Carried by Analogy, Causal and Payoff. Tinbergen's Questions are asked of one system and have no station with many components exchanging messages.

crossToolLinks: K-2: Analogy Mapping of two machines and Tinbergen's timer cards both ask who wrote the rule. Children carry that question into the first Causal Mapping chain as its first card.
3-5: Tracing stored values in a causal map builds the habit that the Tinbergen card's mechanism question asks for, on a different program each time.
6-8: The thermostat map (Analogy Mapping) names a delay and a loop. The traffic-jam map (Causal Mapping) then draws a loop as arrows with signs, and the break column feeds the loop labels.
6-8: The rule that halves a device's rate after a drop is a balancing loop. After filling the link matrix (Payoff Matrices), students redraw that rule as a causal map.
9-12: The video recommender is the same case in the Causal station and the Tinbergen station. The map draws the loop and its delay, and the questions add development and version history.
9-12: The 'who set the objective' row of the three-way map (Analogy Mapping) is the row that the pricing matrix (Payoff Matrices) changes when it adds a price floor.
9-12: The route app is the case of the Tinbergen station and the route finder is the case of the Analogy station. It is one kind of system seen through two tools.
reviewNotes: Everything here is AI-drafted and has not been reviewed by a subject expert. No station has been tested in a classroom.
Evidence for all four tools below age 11 is thin. The K-2 and 3-5 stations rest on studies of component skills, and S72 is known by its title only.

Check the Tinbergen translation first. Rahwan et al. (2019) ground mechanism, development, function and evolution, and group them as how versus why, which the project deck criticizes. The loop rests on Dewsbury (read through the deck) and on the Brinkmann et al. preprint.

The cultural-history and family-history rows are left out because no software counterpart was found. Design traditions are folded into the version-history question. A reviewer may want a different split.
The payoff stations borrow the table form from the Guide's human examples. Check that no wording drifts into trust, fairness or intention.
Organism wording for machines is avoided throughout, in line with Rahwan et al.'s warning against anthropomorphism and zoomorphism. The Guide's organism wording for language models is not used.

After review 10 of 26 stations carry AI4K12 ids and K-2 carries none. That matches the alignment finding that the K-2 stages have little counterpart in AI4K12. The alignment is thin, so it should not be presented as dense.
Search appears in the AI4K12 sense (path from start to goal) in the route app only. No list-search item carries an AI4K12 id.
Traffic recurs in five stations (pedestrian light, traffic-light model, traffic model, buses, route app). Consider swapping one for a text or data example.

The reviewer found content errors that were fixed: a traffic chain drawn as a reinforcing loop, a link game that shows a dilemma only under particular settings, and a remix station that never asked the first three Tinbergen questions.

int.aimFit: The aim is transfer across domains with an honest statement of where it stops. Analogy maps and Tinbergen's grid ask one set of questions of biology, culture, technology, education, AI and computation, and cognition, and their break columns and empty rows come from the vocabulary's 'does not carry over' notes. Two 9-12 stations, a payoff table and a feed map, show that feedback, incentive and fitness change meaning by domain. The boundary forbids wants, intent or a family for machines. Every analogy map carries a break column.
int.sequence: Analogy leads at K-2 and shares the lead at 3-5 with Tinbergen and Causal. Card comparisons grow into maps with a break column, while Causal and Payoff begin as arrow cards and outcome tables. At 6-8 Tinbergen and Causal share the lead, and Causal adds delays to the loops begun at 3-5. At 9-12 Tinbergen and Analogy share the lead with three or more senses, including machine behaviour and machine culture. Payoff tests choices from 6-8.

tinbergen.roleReason: The grid is the main way Interdisciplinary asks one question of an animal, a person and a machine, and it shows which rows change meaning. It leads at 9-12 and shares the lead with Causal at 6-8, where students have enough sense of time and cause to use it. Younger bands get a reduced form.
tinbergen.form: The full expanded grid across domains: mechanism, development, evolutionary history, cultural history and family history, each with inside and outside causes, plus the function question. Rows are renamed for each domain; for machines they become inputs and rules, training and updates, and the lineage of versions. Rows that do not apply are marked empty with a reason. Younger bands use two or three rows.
tinbergen.mustNotImport: No station calls a language model or an app a species with offspring, and no machine gets wants or a family. The Guide's wording appears only inside the analogy tool, with a breakdown column. Near and far causes are never ranked by importance, and how-versus-why is not taught as the grid's meaning.

stations.move: Children place picture cards for a family trait and a family recipe on a three-part strip: now, when I was little, long ago in the family. For each card they answer: what is happening now, and where did it come from? They sort each card into 'came with me' or 'someone showed me', and spot how two cousins' soups differ. An adult writes the answers.
stations.example: Curly hair that runs in a family, and a grandmother's soup recipe that two cousins both cook.
stations.representation: Picture cards on a strip: now, when I was little, long ago.
stations.challenge: First sorting of causes by when they happened. The function question stays out, because young children give purpose answers for traits.

stations.move: Students watch a clip of a young animal learning from an adult and ask three questions: what set it off just now, how did it get here (practice, watching, whatever help it got), and where did the habit come from (the group's way over many years). They repeat the questions for a child learning a skill and name one difference between the helpers.
stations.example: A young chimpanzee learning to crack nuts by watching its mother, and a child learning to tie shoelaces.
stations.representation: Three-row chart with picture clues and one sticky note per cause.
stations.challenge: Keep a trigger now apart from a cause during growing up and a cause over many years, with one sticky note per cause.

stations.move: Students order picture cards of a writing tool on a timeline and say what each version kept from the one before and what changed. They then ask what outcome the tool creates for people today and why people still use it. The teacher records any answer that gives the tool a purpose of its own.
stations.example: Writing tools over centuries: charcoal, quill, pencil, ballpoint pen.
stations.representation: Timeline of picture cards with a 'kept' note and a 'changed' note under each.
stations.challenge: Add a cultural-history row: causes that reach back decades to centuries, with dates put in order on a timeline.

stations.move: Students ask the history and function questions of two traits side by side. They write biological history and cultural history as separate rows, then answer why does it exist today for each trait, saying what was kept and who or what did the keeping. They also ask whether chance could explain why a trait persists.
stations.example: Beak shape in a finch population, and a swipe feature kept across versions of a phone app.
stations.representation: Two-column grid with rows from mechanism to function and inside and outside boxes.
stations.challenge: Keep the biological and cultural history rows apart, mark the row that stays empty for each trait and say why, and answer the function question separately.

stations.move: Students fill the grid for earthworms that loosen soil, once for the soil change and once for a later worm that is well suited to it. They split each row into inside causes (body, growth) and outside causes (soil, weather, other worms). They test each why answer: does it say what a worm meant to do, or what happened across generations?
stations.example: Earthworms mixing and loosening soil so that later worms and plants do better.
stations.representation: Grid with inside and outside boxes and an arrow from the outside box to later generations.
stations.challenge: Split rows into inside and outside causes, and see that an organism's action can become an outside cause for later generations.

stations.move: Students ask the same questions of three cases in one three-column grid. For the algorithm they rename the rows: inputs and rules, training data and updates, lineage of versions, and what builders and users gain. They mark rows that stay empty and write why. The machine column follows Rahwan et al.'s four classic questions.
stations.example: Bird song, a student's habit of checking a feed, and a video recommendation algorithm.
stations.representation: Three-column grid with renamed rows and empty cells marked with a reason.
stations.challenge: Say, row by row, where a question stops meaning the same thing for animals, people and machines.

stations.move: Students take one social media platform and ask the cultural-history and function questions. How did its features get kept across versions, who chooses what spreads, and what does it do for users and for builders? They then draw the loop from what users do back to what the next version shows. This follows Brinkmann et al. on variation, transmission and selection.
stations.example: The ranking feature of a short-video app across five years of versions.
stations.representation: Row grid plus a looped arrow from 'what users do' to 'next version'.
stations.challenge: Add the loop from consequences back to what gets kept, with a human decision at every turn.

stations.move: Students turn the grid on a habit of thought: explaining a trait by need. They ask what triggers the habit under time pressure, how it develops in childhood, how everyday language keeps it, and what it does for the thinker. They then rewrite one explanation using variation and selection.
stations.example: The sentence 'giraffes grew long necks because they needed to reach leaves'. The cause of long necks is debated, so the rewrite is one hypothesis.
stations.representation: Five-row grid applied to one sentence, with the rewritten sentence beside it.
stations.challenge: Use the grid on one's own thinking, and judge each answer by its row so that a function answer stops standing in for a mechanism answer.

tinbergen.teachingPrompt: Which row is this answer in: what is happening now, how it grew, how it was passed on, or what it does for them? Does that row mean the same thing for an animal, a person and a machine?
gaps: No study found teaches the full grid to children under 11. The K-2 and 3-5 stations rest on studies of component skills such as sorting by time and learning selection from storybooks.

Rahwan et al. ground the four classic questions at three scales. Brinkmann et al. ground variation, transmission and selection in machine culture and never mention Tinbergen. The cultural-history and family-history rows rest on the deck and the human-behaviour literature.

Tinbergen, Dewsbury, Laland and Bateson were known only through the deck's quotations and Rahwan's citations. Ariew and Panchanathan, the source for adding agency, were not read and no station cites them. Evidence from school students on the agency, cultural-history and family-history rows is thin.

causal.roleReason: Causal maps carry the loop and delay ideas that Feedback, Niche Construction and Selection Pressure need. At 9-12 the feed map marks which arrows people decide, a program computes or nobody designed. A grid answer or an analogy often becomes an arrow. Evidence for loops under age 11 is thin.
causal.form: Factors joined by arrows with plus and minus signs, loops, delays and named archetypes. A factor may be a count, a behaviour, a rule, a design or a stored value, and each map labels which kind each factor is. An arrow keeps one meaning per map; where the meaning changes between domains, the map marks the arrow. Points where people could act are named for human systems only.
causal.mustNotImport: No arrow gives a population, a gene or a program a goal, and no loop is read as foresight. Arrows that change meaning between domains (an animal's response, a person's reason, a designer's setting) are marked and never merged. Explanations of group patterns by a hidden controller are challenged.

stations.move: Children link picture cards with string to show what a bird needs and what it does: hungry, looks for food, finds food, feeds chicks, chicks grow, chicks look for food too. They say 'this makes that happen' for each pair. The teacher adds a return arrow only if a child notices that the story comes back to the start.
stations.example: A bird that looks for food, feeds its chicks, and has chicks that look for food in turn.
stations.representation: Picture cards joined by string and arrows, one cause for each arrow.
stations.challenge: First arrows between factors: one cause for one effect, with a return arrow shown only when a child spots it.

stations.move: Students map a shared class resource. They draw arrows from who uses it to how much is left to how people feel, and find one cycle: less paint, more grabbing, even less paint. Each arrow gets a plus or minus. They compare a map for a class with a turn-taking rule that others expect and uphold with a map for a class without one.
stations.example: A paint set shared by two table groups, with taking turns or grabbing.
stations.representation: Factor cards with plus and minus arrows on a table-size poster.
stations.challenge: Close one loop: an effect that returns to its own cause, with one sign on each arrow.

stations.move: Students map a learner and a helper. Skill rises with practice, help falls as skill rises, and a slip in skill brings help back. They act it out with a paper bicycle, then draw the same shape for a meerkat pup and an adult who hands over prey in easier and harder forms. They say which helper acts on purpose.
stations.example: A child learning to ride a bicycle while a helper lets go a little at a time.
stations.representation: Moving cards on a poster; arrows marked plus or minus.
stations.challenge: Read a balancing loop: help falls as skill rises. Students check the sign on each arrow aloud.

stations.move: Students map how a class library of solved examples speeds up later problems. Each solved problem adds an example, a new problem starts from the closest solved example, and faster work adds more examples. They mark the delay, because the library helps later problems and leaves the present one alone, and predict how the curve bends.
stations.example: A class worked-example library that grows as each problem is solved.
stations.representation: Factor cards with plus arrows, a loop and a delay mark.
stations.challenge: Add a delay: the effect arrives later than the cause. Students mark it and predict how the growth bends.

stations.move: Students map how keeping cattle changed human life: herds give milk, milk use raises the advantage of adults who digest it, and such adults may keep more herds (an arrow to test). They mark which arrows act within a lifetime and which act across generations, and give the slow arrows a delay mark. No arrow carries a plan to evolve.
stations.example: Herding families, milk in the diet, and the spread of milk digestion in adults.
stations.representation: Factor cards with plus arrows, delay marks and two arrow colours: fast and slow.
stations.challenge: Separate fast arrows (one lifetime) from slow ones (across generations) and read a loop that has no planner in it.

stations.move: Students map how a word for a game spreads and fades. Children hear it, some copy it, copying makes it more common, and when children stop passing it on it ends. A chance arrow (who happens to be copied early) sits beside a reason arrow (a popular older child). They ask which arrow a table of counts could tell apart.
stations.example: A local word for a playground game, spreading through a town and then fading as children stop passing it on.
stations.representation: Factor cards with a reason arrow and a chance arrow shown in different colours.
stations.challenge: Show chance and bias as two separate arrows into one outcome, and say what evidence could tell them apart.

stations.move: Students map how a crowd's average guess can beat most members: independent guesses go in, averaging comes out, and an arrow from seeing others' guesses on a shared tally board can break it. They add the copying loop and test it by running a counting game twice, once with private guesses and once with the board in view. No arrow comes from a leader.
stations.example: Guessing the beans in a jar, with and without seeing others' guesses.
stations.representation: Factor cards and arrows, with the copying loop drawn in a second colour.
stations.challenge: Explain a group result with no controller in the map, and find the arrow that turns a helpful loop into a harmful one.

stations.move: Students draw the loop between readers, a ranking system and the people who write for it. Clicks become training data, training data changes what is shown, and what is shown changes clicks and what writers make. They add an arrow for a designer's setting, mark who holds the power to change it, and label each arrow decided, computed or undesigned.
stations.example: A news-ranking feed, its readers and the writers who adjust headlines to it.
stations.representation: Factor cards, arrows with signs, and three arrow styles: decided, computed, undesigned.
stations.challenge: Mark which arrows people decide, which the program computes and which no one designed, and look for an amplifying loop.

causal.teachingPrompt: Where does an effect come back to its own cause? Who or what decides that arrow: a person, a rule someone wrote, or nobody?
gaps: No study found teaches causal maps with loops to children under 11. K-2 rests on studies of causal learning in preschoolers and on a bee unit; 3-5 on a few small classroom studies.

Most evidence on drawing and reading maps with delays comes from middle school and adults, and adults do poorly on stocks, flows and delays. The 9-12 stations are a bet that older students do better with explicit teaching of loop types.
The project's own causal-mapping paper was not read in full here.

payoff.roleReason: Payoff tables fit only the concepts about choices between parties: Cooperation, Conflict, Incentive, Norms, Fitness. Evidence for reading two-party tables under age 11 is thin, so K-2 and 3-5 use outcome tables. The tool earns a place because it shows that a payoff means different things in biology, culture and software.
payoff.form: A table of outcomes for each pair of choices by two parties. What a payoff is depends on the sense: offspring left by a strategy (biology), costs and benefits as people judge them (culture), a score a designer set (AI and computation). Early bands start with outcome tables and short words. Every table says whose choice it is and whether choice is the right word.
payoff.mustNotImport: No table gives bacteria, bees or programs reasons, trust or fairness. Fitness payoffs are never read as one animal's choice, and a designer's reward is never read as what a program wants. Human cases are not used as evidence for what evolved. Calling a human case a game comes with its breakdown column.

stations.move: Children act out a two-choice classroom situation: share the blocks or keep them all. They fill a picture table with face cards for what happens to me after each choice, first for one child, then for the pair. Children say what each child wanted, then check whether the table matches.
stations.example: Two children and one box of blocks at choosing time.
stations.representation: Picture table with face cards, one row per choice.
stations.challenge: First outcome table: one choice and its result for me and for the other child. Long-term columns are left out.

stations.move: Students fill a two-by-two table of words for two classes that share one playground ball in a rainy week. Each class can take the ball every break or take turns. Cells say what happens to each class. A second column asks what happens next week. Results are compared across groups, since classes differ.
stations.example: Two classes and one playground ball in a rainy week.
stations.representation: Two-by-two table of short sentences with a 'next week' column.
stations.challenge: Two parties with two choices each, and one extra column for later. Evidence for this age is thin, so the teacher watches closely.

stations.move: Students fill a table for two fishers who share a lake: each can take many fish or few, with columns for this season and for ten years on. They find the dilemma, then test two ways out: a norm that members uphold by approval, and a rule with a fine. They name which party holds which kind of power to change the table.
stations.example: Two fishers sharing one lake.
stations.representation: Two-by-two table with short-term and long-term columns, and a second table after each change.
stations.challenge: Find the dilemma in the gap between the short-term and long-term columns, then test two ways out. Evidence for this skill at age 12 is thin.

stations.move: Students fill a payoff table for two bird types that meet at a food patch: one fights, one backs off. Each cell shows the average chicks raised. They read which type leaves more chicks against which, then ask how each type's share of the population shifts over generations. They state that no bird reads the table.
stations.example: Birds that fight over a food patch and birds that back off.
stations.representation: Two-by-two table of average chicks, plus a bar for each type's share over generations.
stations.challenge: Read a payoff as offspring left by a type, add a population column, and see that no individual chooses.

stations.move: Students fill one dilemma table three times with the same shape: fitness for two inherited strategies, costs and benefits for two neighbours, and a designer's reward for two programs sharing a server. They compare what choice means in each column and what could change the result: selection over generations, talk and rules, or editing the reward.
stations.example: A shared-resource dilemma read as animal strategies, neighbours' water use and two programs' rewards.
stations.representation: Three copies of one table, with a strip below each: what is a payoff, what is a choice.
stations.challenge: Compare three meanings of payoff and choice in one table shape, and say which fix works in each.

stations.move: Students play a repeated two-choice game on a payoff table, first against a classmate and then against a program with a simple stated rule. After each round they write what they expect the other side to do and why, then check the default picture of the other side they started with. They compare how a person and a program revise their play.
stations.example: A repeated two-choice game against a classmate, then against a rule-following program.
stations.representation: Payoff table plus a round-by-round log: my guess about the other side, what happened.
stations.challenge: Reason about the classmate's picture of you, and state what a rule-following program has in its place. Notice one's own default assumption about the other side.

payoff.teachingPrompt: Who is choosing here, and is choosing the right word? What counts as a good outcome in this table: chicks, something people value, or a score someone set?
gaps: No study found tests whether students can spot a social dilemma from a payoff table. The nearest evidence is on fairness choices, rational choice, delay discounting and strategic play.

The cited studies are adjacent evidence. S49 used college-age players, S44 and S46 covered seven and six societies, and S52 and S53 measured delay and impulse control. None tests reading a payoff table, so the 6-8 and 9-12 moves are bets.
Cooperation results come from a few societies, and costly sharing differs by culture. Results from Saxony classrooms may differ from the cited figures.
The 9-12 three-reading table has no direct study behind it. It rests on the vocabulary's separate senses of Incentive and Fitness.
Four of six stations are share-or-take dilemmas. A coordination case would widen the range.

analogy.roleReason: Interdisciplinary exists to carry a concept across domains and to say where it stops. An analogy map with a break column does both, and its break cells are the vocabulary's own 'does not carry over' notes. It leads at K-2 and 3-5 with concrete cards, and returns at 9-12 with three or more senses.
analogy.form: Two or more cases from different domains side by side, shared relations in rows, and a 'where it breaks' column filled from the vocabulary's 'does not carry over' notes, with the concept named. Selection, Inheritance and Scaffolding have no such note, so a map names the neighbouring note it borrows. A map is a hypothesis that needs separate evidence. K-2 starts with picture cards sorted into same job, looks alike and different.
analogy.mustNotImport: No map treats surface resemblance as evidence, and no map ends without a break column. 'Species' and 'offspring' for language models appear only as quoted words under test in the one 9-12 map. A machine is never given wants or a family. Each map names the senses it joins.

stations.move: Children put a known case and a new case side by side as picture cards and say what the new one reminds them of. They sort the features into same job, looks alike and different. An adult helps them name one difference, and relation words such as keeps safe help them see the shared job.
stations.example: A bird's nest and a child's pillow fort, both built as a shelter.
stations.representation: Two picture cards and three sorting mats: same job, looks alike, different.
stations.challenge: Name one difference between two cases that share a job, as the Analogical Reasoning note asks. Relation words help; naming a break is untested at this age.

stations.move: Children compare an animal finding food with a toy robot rolling to its charger. On picture cards they sort what is the same (it ends up where it is needed) and what differs (a person built the robot and set its goal, from the Agency note). The teacher asks what rule the robot follows and records any answer that says it wants something.
stations.example: A bird finding seeds and a toy robot rolling to its charger.
stations.representation: Two picture cards and a 'who set it up?' sticker for each.
stations.challenge: Ask for the rule a machine follows when a child says it wants something. Easy tasks draw rule answers; harder tasks draw wants.

stations.move: Students fill a two-column map: a trait passing from parent to child, and the rules of a game passing from one group of children to another. Rows: who holds it, who gets it, how it moves, what can change on the way, how exact the copy is. The break column uses the Transmission note on how exact each copy is.
stations.example: Eye colour passing to a child, and a playground game's rules passing to a new class.
stations.representation: Two-column table with five shared rows and a break column.
stations.challenge: Match on relations such as holder and receiver. Name one break taken from the Transmission note.

stations.move: Students map three learners: a kitten learning to hunt, a child learning to read and a program that sorts photos after seeing labelled examples. Rows: what changes, what experience drives it, who sets the goal, who helps. Each break cell is filled from the Learning and Teaching notes. They also run a small sorting activity with labelled cards.
stations.example: A kitten learning to hunt, a child learning to read and a photo-sorting program trained on labelled pictures.
stations.representation: Three-column table with four rows and a break cell for each pair.
stations.challenge: Three cases instead of two. Break cells compare the program with each living learner, taken from the Learning note.

stations.move: Students map an essay revised over three drafts against a bird population changing over generations. Rows: what varies, what keeps or drops versions, what is passed on. The break column uses the Evolutionary Process note: one writer revising is not a population, the writer aims at a goal, and mutations ignore need. They list essay-side words that do not fit the birds.
stations.example: A student revising an essay over three drafts and a bird population over many generations.
stations.representation: Two-column table with three relation rows and a break column with the concept named.
stations.challenge: Check the map against a second analogy, a breeder choosing animals, since one analogy can leave a wrong picture. Name where the first one fails.

stations.move: Students compare three stand-ins for one school: a floor plan, a child's mental picture and a robot's stored grid of corridors. Rows: what is kept, what is left out, who treats it as a stand-in. The break column uses the Representation note: a map is not the territory, and a stored grid means nothing to the program alone.
stations.example: A school floor plan, a child's mental picture of the school and a robot's stored corridor grid.
stations.representation: Three-column table with rows for kept, left out and who reads it.
stations.challenge: Say who treats each item as a stand-in and what each leaves out, then name a use for which each would fail.

stations.move: Students map three cases of selection: a breeder choosing pigeons, a wild finch population and a genetic algorithm. Rows: the variants, what keeps them, what passes on, who sets the target. The break column cites the Fitness, Evolutionary Process and Domestication notes, because Selection has none. They compare with Darwin's use of the breeder analogy and check each wording for need-based phrases.
stations.example: A breeder choosing pigeons, a wild finch population and a genetic algorithm, set beside Darwin's use of the breeder analogy.
stations.representation: Three-column table with four rows and a break column that names the concept.
stations.challenge: Join three cases in one map and set it beside Darwin's use of the breeder analogy. Name the wrong picture each single case would leave.

stations.move: Students test the Guide's quoted words 'species' and 'offspring' for language models. They map species and offspring against model versions and derivatives, filling the break column first from the Descent, Population, Transmission and Evolutionary Process notes: mixed lines, no interbreeding, exact or imitated copies, people choosing which versions live. Then they keep or drop each word.
stations.example: A tree of species beside a lineage of language-model versions, where one update can reach millions of copies at once.
stations.representation: Two-column table with the break column filled first and a keep-or-drop list of words.
stations.challenge: Fill the break column before the match column, then test the kept words on a second case, a family tree of tool designs. Keep a word only if it survives both.

stations.move: Students compare how a honeybee swarm picks a nest site with how a school council picks a rule. Rows: shared interest, who gathers information, how options are compared, how agreement is reached, who has influence. The break column uses the Collective Intelligence note: bees have no leader and no plan, and human groups can copy each other or follow a loud voice.
stations.example: A honeybee swarm choosing a nest site and a school council choosing a rule.
stations.representation: Two-column table with the Guide's decision principles as rows and a break column.
stations.challenge: Test each row for a hidden difference: planning, talk and written rules exist in the human column only.

analogy.teachingPrompt: Which rows match because the relations are the same, and which only because the pictures look alike? Where does the map break, and which note says so?
gaps: No study found teaches analogy maps with a named break column to students under 11. Naming where an analogy breaks is untested at K-2 and 3-5, and grade 11 students mostly saw models as copies.

The 9-12 language-model map uses the Teacher's Guide wording as an analogy under test. The Guide puts 'species' and 'offspring' in quotation marks. Neither Rahwan et al. nor Brinkmann et al. use species language for machines, and Rahwan et al. warn against excessive anthropomorphism and zoomorphism. S8 and S9 are cited for these limits and do not support the wording.
Selection, Inheritance and Scaffolding have no 'does not carry over' note, so maps on them borrow the Fitness, Evolutionary Process, Domestication, Transmission, Learning or Teaching notes.
The K-2 robot station rests on small studies (six kindergartners in one, sixty children aged 4 to 7 in another).

coverage.Representation: Analogy carries it at 6-8. Causal carries it at K-2 as the conventions of picture cards and arrows. Grid and payoff stations use representations without teaching how a stand-in works.
coverage.Abstraction: Analogy (6-8) and the 9-12 payoff station, where one table shape is kept and the domain detail dropped, carry it. Tinbergen and Causal use abstraction without making it the thing students study.
coverage.Model: Analogy (6-8) and one Causal station (9-12) carry it. A grid answer is rarely run forward or revised, so Tinbergen and Payoff do not teach the model idea.
coverage.Distributed Cognition: Carried by Causal 9-12 only, and marginally. A cockpit or shared-notes case that splits a task across people and tools would add a second tool.
coverage.Collective Intelligence: Carried by Causal and Analogy at 9-12 only. Payoff tables describe choices between two parties, so they cannot show a group result without a controller.
coverage.Domestication: Carried by Causal (6-8) and Analogy (9-12, as breeding). Payoff and the grid reach it only through Niche Construction and Selection.
coverage.Extinction: Carried by Causal 6-8 only. The Extinction note leaves software and file-format obsolescence out, so the language-model station cannot carry it. A station on a language or a technique that is lost would add a second tool.
coverage.Power: Carried by Payoff (6-8) and Causal (9-12). It has no honest place in the grid stations, and the analogy maps use the Group and Role notes instead.
coverage.Role: Carried by Causal (3-5) and Analogy (9-12). Payoff tables name parties and leave out roles, and the grid stations ask about causes of a trait.
coverage.Institutions: Carried by Payoff (6-8) and Analogy (9-12). The concept is mainly human, so the grid and Causal stations meet it only through Norms.
coverage.Theory of Mind: Carried by Payoff (K-2 and 9-12) and Analogy (K-2). Causal maps have no arrow for another mind's beliefs, and the grid asks about causes of traits.
coverage.Knowledge: Carried by Causal 6-8 only, because no station asks what grounds a claim or who holds it. Adding Knowledge to the 9-12 bee swarm and council analogy would add a second tool.

crossToolLinks: Tinbergen (video recommendation algorithm) and Causal (news-ranking feed) both treat a ranking system at I2:9-12. Read them as one kind of case seen through two tools: the grid sorts its causes and the map draws its loop.
Tinbergen's 9-12 platform station hands its last step, the loop from consequences back to what gets kept, to the Causal feed map, where each arrow is marked as decided, computed or undesigned.
Tinbergen 3-5 (chimpanzee and child learning) and Analogy 3-5 (kitten, child, photo-sorting program) both ask who helps a learner. The Analogy break column carries the Teaching and Learning notes.
Causal 9-12 (jar-counting crowd) and Analogy 9-12 (honeybee swarm and school council) both explain a group result with no controller. Run the crowd game first, then use the map to say what bees lack.
Payoff 6-8 (birds at a food patch) and Tinbergen 6-8 (finch beak and app feature) both use birds. The table reads offspring left by a type, and the grid asks why a trait exists today.
Causal 3-5 (paint set) and Payoff 3-5 (playground ball) show one shared-object case through two tools. Run the map first for the loop, then the table for the choices.
At I2:3-5 the learner with a helper appears in a Tinbergen, a Causal and an Analogy station. Run the grid for who helps, the map for what changes and the analogy to compare learners.
At 9-12 the ranking feed appears in two Tinbergen stations and one Causal station. Run the grid one question at a time, then draw the map.
reviewNotes: Everything here is AI-drafted and has not been reviewed by a subject expert. No classroom has tested any station. All 'canDo' ranges in the evidence file are bets to test.

Evidence is thin for all four tools at K-2 and 3-5. No study found teaches the full grid, causal maps with loops, two-party payoff tables or analogy maps with named break points to children under 11. Check the K-2 and 3-5 stations first.

Rahwan et al. ground only the four classic questions at three scales, and Brinkmann et al. (preprint only) ground variation, transmission and selection in machine culture and never mention Tinbergen. The cultural-history and family-history rows rest on the deck and the human-behaviour literature. Ariew and Panchanathan were not read.

Rahwan et al. group mechanism and development as how, and function and evolution as why. The deck argues against that grouping. The stations use the four-question wording and never teach how-versus-why as the meaning of the grid.

The vocabulary has no 'does not carry over' note for Selection, Inheritance or Scaffolding. Stations that map selection cite the Fitness and Evolutionary Process notes instead. Check that this is acceptable.
Several payoff claims rest on adult or few-society samples (strategic reasoning, delay discounting, fairness across societies). Saxony classrooms may differ.
The 9-12 stations in all four tools lean on university and adult studies. Evidence from school students on agency, cultural-history and family-history rows is thin.
The Guide's words species and offspring appear in quotation marks, only in one 9-12 Analogy station, as a wording under test. The project lead decides whether any space keeps them.
After review only 4 stations keep an AI4K12 id, all at K-2 and 3-5. A 6-8 or 9-12 station would need to ask about training data, search or learning types to earn one. The alignment is thin.

Examples the reviewer found loose and a biologist or teacher should check: 'feel safe' for a bird, 'help that fades' for a chimpanzee, the bird chain that skips feeding, 'predict the swing' for a loop with only plus arrows, the return arrow in the milk map (a hypothesis), the giraffe neck (debated) and pigeons in Darwin's notebooks.
Payoff evidence is adjacent only: adult and few-society samples on strategic reasoning, delay and fairness. None tests a payoff table, so the 6-8 and 9-12 payoff moves are bets.

sources.supports: Two cases of students writing individual-level rules in agent-based models and testing the group-level result; the authors argue this brings advanced topics into high school.

sources.citation: Fehr, E., Bernhard, H., & Rockenbach, B. (2008). Egalitarianism in young children. Nature.
sources.supports: At ages 3 to 4 most children chose selfishly, and by ages 7 to 8 most preferred allocations that remove advantageous or disadvantageous inequality.

sources.citation: Blake, P. R., McAuliffe, K., Corbit, J., et al. (2015). The ontogeny of fairness in seven societies. Nature.
sources.supports: Children aged 4 to 15 in seven societies all rejected disadvantageous inequity by middle childhood, while rejecting advantageous inequity appeared in only three societies and later.

sources.citation: Blake, P. R., & McAuliffe, K. (2011). "I had so much it didn't seem fair": Eight-year-olds reject two forms of inequity. Cognition.
sources.supports: Children aged 4 to 7 rejected offers that left them with less and accepted offers that left them with more, and 8-year-olds rejected both.

sources.citation: House, B. R., Silk, J. B., Henrich, J., et al. (2013). Ontogeny of prosocial behavior across diverse societies. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.
sources.supports: In six societies with children aged 3 to 14, costly prosocial acts dropped in middle childhood and then diverged by society, while costless prosocial acts rose steadily.

sources.citation: Sutter, M., Zoller, C., & Glätzle-Rützler, D. (2019). Economic behavior of children and adolescents: A first survey of experimental economics results. European Economic Review.
sources.supports: Surveys experiments with children and adolescents on choice rationality, risk, time and social preferences, cooperation and competitiveness, by age and gender.

sources.citation: Harbaugh, W. T., Krause, K., & Berry, T. R. (2001). GARP for kids: On the development of rational choice behavior. American Economic Review.
sources.supports: Seven-year-olds showed clear but inconsistent rationality in choices among goods; about 25 percent of 7-year-olds and 60 percent of 11-year-olds passed one test, with no rise from 11 to 21 (read from the working paper text).

sources.citation: Hedden, T., & Zhang, J. (2002). What do you think I think you think? Strategic reasoning in matrix games. Cognition.
sources.supports: College-age adults predicting another player in two-choice matrix games used a default model of the other player and revised it as evidence arrived.

sources.citation: Wellman, H. M., Cross, D., & Watson, J. (2001). Meta-analysis of theory-of-mind development: The truth about false belief. Child Development.
sources.supports: A meta-analysis of 178 studies found a consistent developmental pattern in false-belief performance through the preschool years, across countries and task variations.

sources.citation: Flobbe, L., Verbrugge, R., Hendriks, P., & Krämer, I. (2008). Children's application of theory of mind in reasoning and language. Journal of Logic, Language and Information.
sources.supports: Forty children aged 8 to 10 and 27 adults did second-order false-belief, strategic game and sentence tasks, and children differed from adults.

sources.citation: Steinberg, L., Graham, S., O'Brien, L., Woolard, J., Cauffman, E., & Banich, M. (2009). Age differences in future orientation and delay discounting. Child Development.
sources.supports: In 935 people aged 10 to 30, younger adolescents more often took smaller sooner rewards than people aged 16 and older, and planning ahead kept developing into young adulthood.

sources.citation: Steinbeis, N., Bernhardt, B. C., & Singer, T. (2012). Impulse control and underlying functions of the left DLPFC mediate age-related and age-independent individual differences in strategic social behavior. Neuron.
sources.supports: Children's strategic behavior in two exchange games rose with age, and impulse control explained this better than changes in social preferences.

sources.citation: Gentner, D. (1983). Structure-mapping: A theoretical framework for analogy. Cognitive Science.
sources.supports: Theory that analogies map relations between objects and prefer systems of connected relations over object attributes.

sources.citation: Gentner, D., & Toupin, C. (1986). Systematicity and surface similarity in the development of analogy. Cognitive Science.
sources.supports: Children aged 5 to 7 and 8 to 10 acted out stories with new characters, and how much the new characters resembled the old ones strongly affected transfer.

sources.citation: Gentner, D. (1988). Metaphor as structure mapping: The relational shift. Child Development.
sources.supports: Children interpret metaphors by shared attributes before shared relational structure, with a shift toward relational readings (tested at ages 4 to 10 and in adults).

sources.citation: Kotovsky, L., & Gentner, D. (1996). Comparison and categorization in the development of relational similarity. Child Development.
sources.supports: Six- and eight-year-olds recognized relational similarity across different dimensions, and 4-year-olds did so only with support from lower-order matches.

sources.citation: Goswami, U., & Brown, A. L. (1990). Melting chocolate and melting snowmen: Analogical reasoning and causal relations. Cognition.
sources.supports: Even 3-year-olds solved a:b::c:d analogies when they understood the causal relation involved, such as melting.

sources.citation: Loewenstein, J., & Gentner, D. (2005). Relational language and the development of relational mapping. Cognitive Psychology.
sources.supports: Hearing spatial relational words helped preschoolers map relative positions between two boxes, and the benefit lasted 2 days.

sources.citation: Richland, L. E., Morrison, R. G., & Holyoak, K. J. (2006). Children's development of analogical reasoning: Insights from scene analogy problems. Journal of Experimental Child Psychology.
sources.supports: With ages 3 to 14, performance depended on relational complexity and featural distraction, and the pull of look-alike distractors fell with age.

sources.citation: Gick, M. L., & Holyoak, K. J. (1983). Schema induction and analogical transfer. Cognitive Psychology.
sources.supports: Classic adult study of how comparing analogous cases builds a schema that supports transfer; the abstract was not retrieved.

sources.citation: Alfieri, L., Nokes-Malach, T. J., & Schunn, C. D. (2013). Learning through case comparisons: A meta-analytic review. Educational Psychologist.
sources.supports: A meta-analysis of 57 experiments found case comparison beat single-case and traditional instruction (d about 0.50), most when learners find similarities and receive the principle afterward.

sources.citation: Richland, L. E., & Simms, N. (2015). Analogy, higher order thinking, and education. WIREs Cognitive Science.
sources.supports: Reviews analogy as the base of higher-order thinking in mathematics, science and history education.

sources.citation: Grosslight, L., Unger, C., Jay, E., & Smith, C. L. (1991). Understanding models and their use in science: Conceptions of middle and high school students and experts. Journal of Research in Science Teaching.
sources.supports: Seventh graders and eleventh graders mostly saw models as physical copies of reality, while experts saw them as constructed representations.

sources.citation: Schwarz, C. V., Reiser, B. J., Davis, E. A., et al. (2009). Developing a learning progression for scientific modeling: Making scientific modeling accessible and meaningful for learners. Journal of Research in Science Teaching.
sources.supports: Proposes a learning progression for scientific modeling, illustrated with fifth and sixth graders who built and revised models with explanatory mechanisms.

sources.citation: Coll, R. K., France, B., & Taylor, I. (2005). The role of models and analogies in science education: Implications from research. International Journal of Science Education.
sources.supports: Reviews classroom research showing that models and analogies help most when students build, discuss and critique them.

sources.citation: Spiro, R. J., Feltovich, P. J., Coulson, R. L., & Anderson, D. K. (1989). Multiple analogies for complex concepts: Antidotes for analogy-induced misconception in advanced knowledge acquisition. In Similarity and Analogical Reasoning. Cambridge University Press.
sources.supports: Argues that a single analogy often leaves deeply held wrong ideas in advanced learning and that several analogies counter this.

sources.citation: Pea, R. D. (1986). Language-independent conceptual "bugs" in novice programming. Journal of Educational Computing Research.
sources.supports: Describes persistent novice bugs from primary school to college age, rooted in a superbug: the idea that a hidden mind in the language has intelligent interpretive powers.

sources.citation: Sorva, J. (2013). Notional machines and introductory programming education. ACM Transactions on Computing Education.
sources.supports: Reviews why learning the notional machine, an abstract computer that runs programs, is a major challenge for novices and should be an explicit goal.

sources.citation: Qian, Y., & Lehman, J. (2018). Students' misconceptions and other difficulties in introductory programming. ACM Transactions on Computing Education.
sources.supports: Literature review linking novice programming difficulties to inaccurate mental models, unfamiliar syntax and missing strategies.

sources.citation: Grover, S., & Pea, R. (2013). Computational thinking in K-12: A review of the state of the field. Educational Researcher.
sources.supports: Frames the state of computational thinking in K-12 education and names gaps in the research.

sources.citation: Mioduser, D., Levy, S. T., & Talis, V. (2009). Episodes to scripts to rules: Concrete-abstractions in kindergarten children's explanations of a robot's behavior. International Journal of Technology and Design Education.
sources.supports: Reports that kindergarten children's explanations of a robot's behavior moved from single episodes to scripts to general rules; the abstract was not retrieved, so this rests on the title.

sources.citation: Levy, S. T., & Mioduser, D. (2008). Does it "want" or "was it programmed to..."? Kindergarten children's explanations of an autonomous robot's adaptive functioning. International Journal of Technology and Design Education.
sources.supports: Six kindergarten children used technological or psychological explanations of a robot: easy one-rule tasks drew technological accounts, harder tasks drew psychological ones, and programming experience shifted them back.

sources.citation: Bernstein, D., & Crowley, K. (2008). Searching for signs of intelligent life: An investigation of young children's beliefs about robot intelligence. Journal of the Learning Sciences.
sources.supports: Sixty children aged 4 to 7 began to separate robots from other entities in intellectual and psychological traits as their experience with intelligent technology grew.

sources.citation: Hitron, T., Orlev, Y., Wald, I., et al. (2019). Can children understand machine learning concepts? Proceedings of the 2019 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems.
sources.supports: Children's understanding of basic machine learning improved most when an activity let them work with both data labeling and evaluation (ages not retrieved).

sources.citation: Festerling, J., & Siraj, I. (2020). Alexa, what are you? Exploring primary school children's ontological perceptions of digital voice assistants in open interactions. Human Development.
sources.supports: Focus groups with 27 children aged 6 to 10 examined whether children read a voice assistant's abilities as human-like or machine-like.

sources.citation: Swidan, A., Hermans, F., & Smit, M. (2018). Programming misconceptions for school students. Proceedings of the 2018 ACM Conference on International Computing Education Research.
sources.supports: In 145 Scratch users aged 7 to 17, common misconceptions concerned the order of statements, a variable holding one value at a time and program interactivity, along with high expectations of what a computer can do.

sources.citation: Long, D., & Magerko, B. (2020). What is AI literacy? Competencies and design considerations. Proceedings of the 2020 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems.
sources.supports: Synthesizes a set of AI literacy competencies from the literature; the abstract names no age bands.
